name: Trentino-Alto Adige
tagline: Pale Dolomite spires, apple orchards and dumplings in three languages.
intro: Two provinces share this mountain region. Trentino, to the south, is Italian-speaking, and Alto Adige/Südtirol, to the north, is mostly German-speaking and was Austrian until 1919. Between them they hold the most theatrical part of the Dolomites: pale limestone towers that glow pink at sunset, a phenomenon the Ladin people call enrosadira. Below the peaks are meadows dotted with hay barns, castles on every spur, and valleys lined with apple orchards and vineyards.

Life here mixes Alpine and Mediterranean habits. In Bolzano you might eat speck and Knödel at lunch and drink an espresso under the arcades afterwards. Merano has palm trees and a spa, and Lake Garda's northern tip is lined with olive groves and windsurfers. Infrastructure is superb, with good trains, buses, cable cars and hiking huts, which makes it one of the easiest places in Italy to explore properly without a car.

hero_image.alt: The Sassolungo and Sassopiatto peaks glowing orange at sunset above the Alpe di Siusi meadows
hero_image.credit: Wolfgang Moroder, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

best_time: Come late June to September for hiking, open huts and summer lifts. September and October are golden, with Törggelen wine-and-chestnut feasts. Late November to early January is Christmas-market season, and the ski season runs December to April. Lifts and many huts close from mid-April to early June.
getting_there: Verona and Innsbruck airports are about 1h30 to 2h from Bolzano, and Bolzano itself has a few seasonal flights. The Brenner railway links Verona, Rovereto, Trento and Bolzano with fast trains from Milan, Rome, Munich and Innsbruck, and branch lines run to Merano and up the Val Venosta. Regional buses reach almost every valley, and many hotels include a guest transport pass.

places.name: Val Gardena and the Seceda ridge
places.desc: Ortisei is the base for the Ladin valley of woodcarvers. From there, ride the cable car to Seceda, where the grassy Odle ridge breaks off into a row of jagged spires. Walk down via the Pieralongia meadows and their huts, or cross to the Alpe di Siusi, Europe's largest high-altitude pasture.

image.alt: Green Seceda pastures and huts with the Odle spires and Sella group beyond, Val Gardena
image.credit: NorbertNagel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Bolzano
places.desc: The German-speaking capital of South Tyrol, with arcaded Laubengasse, an open-air fruit market on Piazza delle Erbe and Ötzi the Iceman in the archaeology museum. Ride the cable cars to the Renon plateau to see the earth pyramids, or walk the Oswald promenade above the vineyards at dusk.

image.alt: Piazza Walther in Bolzano with its statue, flower beds and the Gothic cathedral spire
image.credit: Benreis, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Merano
places.desc: A Habsburg-era spa town of Art Nouveau villas, palms and mountain views. Walk the Tappeiner promenade, soak in the Terme Merano pools, and lose an afternoon in the terraced Gardens of Trauttmansdorff Castle, where Empress Sisi wintered. In autumn the Waalwege, paths along old irrigation channels, smell of ripening apples.

image.alt: Merano's rooftops and Gothic church tower below green mountains, seen from the Powder Tower
image.credit: Rolf Kranz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Trento
places.desc: Trento hosted the Council of Trent in the 1500s and kept the frescoed façades to prove it. Look at the Piazza Duomo and Neptune fountain, then see the medieval Months cycle in the Castello del Buonconsiglio. MUSE, Renzo Piano's science museum, is great with kids, and Trentodoc sparkling wine flows at every aperitivo.

image.alt: The Neptune fountain in Trento's Piazza Duomo with the cathedral and civic tower
image.credit: Zairon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Lago di Braies
places.desc: A jade-green lake under the sheer wall of the Croda del Becco, with wooden rowing boats tied to a little boathouse. Walk the flat 3.5-km loop early in the morning. In summer, private-car access is restricted at peak hours, so come by bus or book a parking slot.

image.alt: Lago di Braies at sunrise with its wooden boathouse and mist below the Croda del Becco
image.credit: Walter799, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

places.name: Riva del Garda
places.desc: At Lake Garda's narrow northern tip, cliffs drop straight into the water and the afternoon Ora wind brings out windsurfers and sailors. Climb to the Bastione for the view, swim from the pebble beaches, and ride a bike along the cantilevered cliff path at Limone, just down the shore.

image.alt: Riva del Garda and the northern tip of Lake Garda between steep mountains
image.credit: Stefano Travasci, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

things_to_do.title: Go hut-to-hut in the Dolomites
things_to_do.desc: Walk a few days of the Alta Via 1 or the Puez-Odle circuit, sleeping in rifugi with bunk rooms, hot showers and dinners of polenta and goulash. Book huts months ahead for July and August.

things_to_do.title: Join Törggelen in autumn
things_to_do.desc: From October to November, farm taverns around Bressanone and the Isarco valley serve new wine, roast chestnuts, speck, sauerkraut and Krapfen. Walk there along the Keschtnweg chestnut trail.

things_to_do.title: Meet Ötzi the Iceman
things_to_do.desc: The South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano displays the 5,300-year-old glacier mummy in a chilled cell, along with his copper axe, grass cloak and bearskin cap.

things_to_do.title: Climb a via ferrata
things_to_do.desc: Iron ladders and cables make Dolomite summits possible for fit hikers. Hire a guide in Corvara or Canazei for a first route, such as the Brigata Tridentina on the Sella group.

things_to_do.title: Ride the Renon railway
things_to_do.desc: Take the cable car up from Bolzano, then the little narrow-gauge tram across the Renon plateau to Collalbo. From there, walk to the earth pyramids, clay pillars topped with boulders.

things_to_do.title: Cycle the Val Venosta
things_to_do.desc: Take the train up to Malles, then roll downhill for about 60 km on the cycle path to Merano, through apple orchards and past castles. You can drop rented bikes at any station.

things_to_do.title: Visit the Christmas markets
things_to_do.desc: Bolzano's on Piazza Walther is the biggest, Merano's runs along the river promenade, and Bressanone's fills the cathedral square. Drink Glühwein from the souvenir mug and eat Kiachl.

flavours.name: Speck Alto Adige IGP
flavours.desc: Ham cured with juniper, lightly smoked and air-dried for months. Slice it thick on a wooden board with rye crispbread and a glass of Vernatsch.

flavours.name: Canederli / Knödel
flavours.desc: Bread dumplings bound with egg and milk and flavoured with speck, cheese or spinach. Served in broth or with melted butter and Parmesan.

flavours.name: Schlutzkrapfen
flavours.desc: Half-moon rye ravioli filled with spinach and quark, drowned in brown butter and chives. Every South Tyrolean grandmother has her own version.

flavours.name: Strangolapreti
flavours.desc: Trentino's 'priest-stranglers': spinach-and-bread gnocchi in sage butter. The name comes from a story about greedy clergy at the Council of Trent.

flavours.name: Puzzone di Moena DOP
flavours.desc: A pungent washed-rind cheese from the Fassa and Fiemme valleys, much milder than it smells and wonderful melted.

flavours.name: Apfelstrudel
flavours.desc: Thin pastry rolled around local apples, raisins, pine nuts and cinnamon. Eat it warm with vanilla sauce in a mountain hut.

flavours.name: Trentodoc
flavours.desc: Bottle-fermented mountain sparkling wine from Trentino's Chardonnay and Pinot Nero: crisp, fresh and the region's favourite aperitivo.

flavours.name: Lagrein and Gewürztraminer
flavours.desc: Two South Tyrolean classics: the dark, violet-scented Lagrein red from Bolzano, and the aromatic Gewürztraminer white, which takes its name from the village of Tramin.

flavours.name: Grappa trentina
flavours.desc: Trentino distillers make clean, aromatic grappa from Teroldego, Nosiola and Müller-Thurgau pomace. It's served after a big dinner.

legacy_restaurants.name: Osteria a le Due Spade
legacy_restaurants.desc: Opened to feed delegates to the Council of Trent, it is a tiny, refined dining room steps from the cathedral with an eighteenth-century pine Stube. Expect creative Trentino cooking, such as ricotta gnocchi and lake fish.

legacy_restaurants.name: Wirtshaus Vögele
legacy_restaurants.desc: First recorded in 1277 and run by the Kamaun family since 1840, this is Bolzano's 'living room': panelled Stuben, Knödel trios, goulash and Kaiserschmarrn, with locals at the Stammtisch.

legacy_restaurants.name: Batzen Häusl
legacy_restaurants.desc: An old Teutonic Order tavern, an artists' haunt for centuries, now home to a microbrewery. Drink house-brewed beer in the garden with hearty Tyrolean plates.

stay_local.title: A Roter Hahn farm stay
stay_local.desc: South Tyrol's 'Red Rooster' label certifies working farms with a handful of rooms or apartments. Collect eggs, help with the hay, and eat the farm's own apple juice, speck and cheese at breakfast.

stay_local.title: Agritur Maso il Gioco, Balbido
stay_local.desc: A family farm stay in Balbido, the 'painted village' of the Giudicarie, a short walk from Rango, one of Italy's most beautiful villages. Lunches use the farm's own produce, and in December you can walk to Rango's Christmas market in its old courtyards.

stay_local.title: Sleep in a Dolomite rifugio
stay_local.desc: Huts such as Rifugio Genova (Schlüterhütte), beneath the Odle above Val di Funes, offer bunks, Knödel dinners and sunrise on the peaks. Book ahead for summer weekends, and bring a sleeping-bag liner.

day_trips.desc: Walk the promenades, tour the Trauttmansdorff gardens, and soak in the thermal pools before catching an evening train back to Bolzano.

day_trips.how: About 1h by car or train and bus
day_trips.desc: See the little church of St. Johann in Ranui under the Odle peaks, then walk the Adolf Munkel trail below the cliffs.
Swim at Riva, walk up to the waterfall at Varone, and taste the north shore's olive oil, the most northerly in Italy.

hidden_gems.name: Val di Funes
hidden_gems.desc: A quiet farming valley facing the Odle spires. Its little Baroque church of St. Johann in Ranui, alone in a meadow, has become one of the Dolomites' most loved images. Come early, walk the Adolf Munkel trail, and eat at a valley Gasthof.

image.alt: Green meadows of Val di Funes below the jagged Odle peaks
image.credit: Einaz80, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hidden_gems.name: Lago di Tovel
hidden_gems.desc: Hidden in the Brenta Dolomites in the Adamello-Brenta Nature Park, this lake was famous until the 1960s for turning blood-red in summer from algae. Today it is a calm blue-green, with an easy forest loop around its shore.

image.alt: Still waters of Lago di Tovel reflecting forest and the Brenta Dolomites
image.credit: Llorenzi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hidden_gems.name: Glorenza
hidden_gems.desc: One of the smallest towns in the Alps, Glorenza (Glurns) still sits entirely within its sixteenth-century walls, with three gate towers and arcaded lanes. In autumn, walk the walls and eat in an old Gasthaus in the Val Venosta.

image.alt: The walled town of Glorenza among fields and orchards in the Val Venosta
image.credit: Tilman2007, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

hidden_gems.name: Castel Thun
hidden_gems.desc: This fairy-tale castle above the Val di Non's apple orchards has its rooms intact, including the pine-panelled Bishop's room. On a clear day you can see from the Brenta Dolomites to the Adige valley.

image.alt: View over the orchards of the Val di Non from the walls of Castel Thun
image.credit: Viaggiamocela, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

festivals.name: Christmas markets
festivals.where: Bolzano, Merano, Bressanone, Brunico, Vipiteno, Trento
festivals.desc: The markets, with wooden stalls, carved nativity figures, mulled wine and strudel, are among the best in Europe. Smaller valley markets, such as Rango's in Trentino, are more intimate.

festivals.name: Meraner Traubenfest
festivals.desc: Merano's grape festival dates back to 1886. There are brass bands and Schützen in traditional dress, and a parade of floats decorated with grapes and apples through the spa town.

festivals.name: I Suoni delle Dolomiti
festivals.where: Mountain meadows and huts across Trentino
festivals.desc: Concerts high in the mountains: audiences hike up to listen to world-class musicians playing in pastures and beside huts, sometimes at dawn.

festivals.name: Herz-Jesu-Feuer
festivals.when: Sunday after the feast of the Sacred Heart, June
festivals.desc: At nightfall, hundreds of bonfires shaped like hearts, crosses and symbols blaze on the slopes, a tradition dating back to the wars against Napoleon.

culture: This is the only Italian region with three living languages: Italian, German and, in the Gardena, Badia and Fassa valleys, Ladin, an ancient Rhaeto-Romance language with its own schools and newspapers. Val Gardena's woodcarvers have shaped saints, toys and nativity figures for centuries. Village brass bands, the Musikkapellen, play at every feast, and the Schützen, traditional riflemen's companies, march in feathered hats. In early December, Krampus runs send horned, fur-clad devils through the streets, and Ladin valleys still hold their own carnival masks and harvest rituals.
